pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Ages 5–7 — know that whales and dolphins are mammals, not fish: they breathe air, are warm-blooded, and feed their babies milk, even though they live in the ocean.
• Standards — UK (DfE KS1): Y1 'identify and name a variety of common animals… that are… mammals, fish…' and 'describe and compare the structure of a variety of common animals (… including pets)'; classifying by shared features is the KS1 hook.
• Standards — US (NGSS): supports 1-LS1-2 / 2-LS4-1 reasoning about animal groups and features; the mammal-defining traits (air-breathing, warm-blooded, milk) are the criteria.
• Operational details: this is a CLASSIFY-BY-FEATURE topic whose whole point is defeating a misconception ('lives in water = fish'). Teach the mammal criteria as a checklist the child applies (breathes air at the surface / feeds babies milk / warm-blooded / (usually) has some hair) and contrast directly with a fish (breathes water through gills, lays eggs, cold-blooded, scales). The single most memorable evidence is the blowhole breath and the calf drinking milk.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (~5–6): states a whale/dolphin is a mammal and gives one reason (comes up to breathe); Tier B (~6–7): gives ≥2 mammal reasons and names one contrast with a fish; Tier C (~7): applies the criteria to a new animal (e.g. is a shark a fish or mammal? why?) — reasoning from features, not appearance.
bestPractices: Confront the misconception head-on: start by asking 'is a dolphin a fish?' and let the surprising answer drive the lesson (predict–then–check).
Give a concrete feature CHECKLIST the child applies rather than a label to memorise — breathes air / feeds milk / warm-blooded — so the reasoning transfers to new animals.
Contrast side-by-side with a real fish (gills vs blowhole, eggs vs milk, scales vs smooth skin) so the categories are defined by criteria, not habitat.
Use vivid, verifiable anchors: a whale surfacing to breathe through its blowhole; a calf nursing underwater — these are the memorable proofs.
Connect to what the child already knows: they are a mammal too (they breathe air and drank milk as a baby) — the dolphin is 'like us', not 'like a fish'.
keyRepresentations: A two-column compare chart: MAMMAL (breathes air, milk, warm-blooded) vs FISH (gills, eggs, cold-blooded)
A tick-the-features checklist card the child runs against a mystery animal
A cutaway of a dolphin surfacing to breathe through its blowhole
An image of a whale/dolphin calf nursing to anchor 'feeds babies milk'
commonMisconceptions: 'It lives in water and swims, so it's a fish' — the core habitat-equals-category error this topic exists to fix.
'It has fins, so it's a fish' — classifying by superficial body shape rather than defining features.
'Mammals can't live in water / can't hold their breath that long' — not knowing whales surface to breathe air.
'A shark is a mammal because it's big/smart' — over-applying the new category; sharks are fish (gills, no milk).
Thinking 'warm-blooded' means the animal feels warm to touch, rather than regulating its own body temperature.

learn.summary: For ages 5–7: whales and dolphins are mammals, not fish, because they breathe air at the surface, are warm-blooded, and feed their babies milk — even though they live in the ocean. The teaching target is classification BY FEATURE, deliberately confronting the 'lives in water = fish' misconception. The lead activity has the child run a mammal feature-checklist against several sea animals and sort them; supporting activities provide a side-by-side mammal/fish contrast, an assessment sort, and an optional in-role dialogue spark.

activities.title: Sort the sea animals by feature, not by where they live
feedback: If the child drops the dolphin into FISH, gently block it: 'It lives in water… but look at your checklist — does it breathe air? does it feed its baby milk?' and let them re-drop it into MAMMAL.
When the dolphin is placed correctly, a 'looks like a fish but breathes air!' reveal confirms the insight.

If the child calls the shark a mammal because it is big or lives in the sea, point back to its clues: it breathes with gills and does not feed its babies milk, so it is a fish — the feature test, not size, decides.
If a child reads 'warm-blooded' as 'feels warm to touch', clarify that it means the animal keeps its own body warm even in cold water.
Praise reasoning that names a feature ('milk', 'comes up to breathe') rather than just the right box.
activities.rationale: Classification is itself an act of applying criteria, so having the child recompute the category from ticked features — and feel the correction when the 'lives in water' shortcut fails — is intended to target the misconception and may build reasoning intended to transfer to new animals. Including a true fish (shark) is intended to block over-applying the new mammal category.
sourceClaims: Whales and dolphins are marine mammals: they breathe air through lungs, are warm-blooded, give birth to live young and nurse them with milk — distinguishing them from fish.
UK KS1 Y1 science requires pupils to identify and name a variety of common animals including mammals and fish, and to describe and compare their structure.
learnerActions: Meet a line-up of sea animals — dolphin, whale, seal, shark, cod, clownfish — each shown with tappable feature clues (surfaces to breathe / has gills / calf nursing / lays eggs / keeps its body warm even in cold water).

For each animal, tick the features you find and use a simple checklist to decide: does it come up to breathe air? does it feed its baby milk? does its body stay warm even in cold water? does it have gills?
Drop each animal into the MAMMAL box or the FISH box based on the ticked features, not on the fact that it swims in the sea.

Try the dolphin: tap its blowhole to see it surface and breathe air, and tap the nursing calf — then deliberately leave the shark (it breathes with gills and does not feed its babies milk) in the FISH box to avoid over-generalising.
State out loud: 'A dolphin is a mammal, and two reasons are ___ and ___.'
activities.intendedInsight: The rule that decides mammal vs fish is the animal's defining FEATURES (breathes air, feeds milk, warm-blooded) — not its habitat or body shape. The same test applies to a brand-new animal.

activities.title: Side-by-side: dolphin vs fish, reveal the matching features
feedback: When a flap is lifted, name the trait and its contrasting counterpart so the pair is explicit.
If the child expects the dolphin to have gills, show the blowhole flap: it must surface to breathe and cannot breathe underwater.
If the child thinks 'warm-blooded' means warm to touch, explain it means keeping its body warm even in cold water, unlike a cold-blooded fish.
activities.rationale: A crisp, cheap exposition that presents the contrast clearly. This activity shows the answer rather than having the child do the classifying, so it works best as a lead-in or companion to the sorting task; recognition of a shown contrast does not by itself require the child to classify independently.
sourceClaims: Whales and dolphins are marine mammals: they breathe air through lungs, are warm-blooded, give birth to live young and nurse them with milk — distinguishing them from fish.
learnerActions: Look at a split scene: a dolphin (with blowhole and nursing calf, and that stays warm in cold water) beside a real fish (with gills, eggs, scales).
Tap each hotspot to lift a flap — tap the blowhole → 'breathes air'; tap the calf → 'drinks milk'; tap the gills → 'breathes using water through gills'; tap the eggs → 'lays eggs'.
Say which trait on the dolphin matches which trait on the fish, pairing each mammal feature with its fish counterpart.
activities.intendedInsight: Mammals and fish differ by traits that can be compared one-to-one (blowhole vs gills, milk vs eggs for most fish, keeps-warm vs cold-blooded for most fish), so the categories are set by features, not by where the animal lives.

activities.title: Check and extend: sort, say why, and test a new animal
feedback: If a child answers 'fish' for the dolphin because of fins or swimming, re-run the three mammal tests — breathes air, feeds milk, keeps its body warm — which it passes.
If a child answers 'mammal' for the shark, point to its gills and the fact that it does not feed its babies milk: those features make it a fish.
activities.rationale: A recognition-and-sort check confirms both evidence goals and the transfer step. Recognition responses can confirm understanding but do not by themselves elicit the independent construction that the hands-on sorting and spoken justification provide, so pair it with those.
sourceClaims: UK KS1 Y1 science requires pupils to identify and name a variety of common animals including mammals and fish, and to describe and compare their structure.
learnerActions: Sort a fresh set of animals into mammal vs fish.
Answer 'Why is a dolphin a mammal?' choosing the feature-based reason (breathes air / feeds milk) over a habitat reason.
Tackle a transfer question: 'Is a shark a mammal?' and give the reason from its features (breathes with gills, does not feed its babies milk → fish).
activities.intendedInsight: The learner can independently justify the category with defining features and apply the test to an animal they were not taught directly.

activities.title: Optional spark: ask the dolphin why it keeps surfacing
feedback: Follow the dolphin's answer by connecting it to the child: 'You breathe air too, and you drank milk as a baby — so a dolphin is like you.'
Steer the conversation back to the feature test so the spark leads into sorting or justification.
activities.rationale: A charming, personal hook that may surface the air-breathing evidence and link the animal to the child's own experience. It is a motivational spark, not the main classification mechanism; reliable feature-based sorting is intended to be trained by the hands-on activity, not by the spark alone.
sourceClaims: Whales and dolphins are marine mammals: they breathe air through lungs, are warm-blooded, give birth to live young and nurse them with milk — distinguishing them from fish.
learnerActions: Talk in role to a friendly dolphin (or a marine biologist) and ask 'Why do you keep coming up to the top of the water?'
Hear the dolphin explain: 'I have to breathe air like you — that's why I'm not a fish,' and ask a follow-up about how its baby feeds.
activities.intendedInsight: The air-breathing proof becomes memorable and personal — the dolphin is 'like us', not like a fish.

constraints: The core objective is classification by defining feature; do not let activities reward the 'lives in water = fish' or 'has fins = fish' shortcuts.

Teach the mammal criteria as a checklist the child applies (breathes air at the surface / feeds babies milk / warm-blooded / usually some hair), contrasted with a typical fish (breathes using gills, usually lays eggs, usually cold-blooded, usually has scales); gills are the most reliable fish clue, since some fish such as many sharks give birth to live young.
Always include a true fish such as a shark so the child does not over-apply the new mammal category to any large or clever sea animal.
Clarify 'warm-blooded' means the animal keeps its own body temperature steady (stays warm even in cold water), not that it feels warm to touch; do not present a 'warm to touch' clue.
The side-by-side reveal activity and the recognition quiz show or test the answer; they support but do not replace the child's own act of sorting and spoken justification that builds transfer.

Connect to the child's own mammal traits (breathing air, having drunk milk as a baby) to make the category concrete, without implying mammals cannot live in water — whales are sea mammals, bats are flying mammals.
The dialogue activity is an optional spark; it should not be the sole mechanism for training reliable classification at this age.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; both listed sources are marked verified:false in the row and were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row claimed a sorting interaction is uniquely able to 'dismantle the misconception' and rated 3D as adding 'nothing' and dialogue/quiz as merely showing or checking the answer. These comparative-efficacy and necessity claims are not established by the available sources; they have been softened to scoped affordances/limits (e.g. recognition confirms but does not elicit independent construction).

Minor factual care: the checklist's 'usually has some hair' holds for mammals generally but adult whales/dolphins have very little or no hair — presented as a general mammal cue, not a strong whale/dolphin feature, to avoid confusing young learners.
'Breathes water through gills' is a simplification for this age band (fish actually extract dissolved oxygen from water); retained to match the row's age-level wording.

Warm-bloodedness is hard to represent observably for ages 5–7; the 'stays warm even in cold water' clue approximates temperature regulation and deliberately avoids a 'warm to touch' cue, which the row flags as a misconception. Air-breathing and milk-feeding remain the two strongest, most verifiable anchors.

probeDeeper: 'Why does a dolphin have to keep coming up to the top of the water — what would happen if it couldn't?'
'A shark also lives in the sea and has fins. Is a shark a fish or a mammal — and how is it different from a dolphin?' (near-miss counterexample: shark IS a fish)
'How does a baby dolphin feed — and what does that tell you about what kind of animal it is?'
'Does living in the water decide whether an animal is a fish? Give me your reason.'
assess.correctAnswer: It's not right — a dolphin (and a whale) is a MAMMAL, not a fish, even though it lives in the sea. You can tell because it breathes AIR: it has to come up to the surface to breathe and cannot breathe underwater. It is also warm-blooded, and it feeds its babies milk. Living in water and having fins does not make an animal a fish.

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks anything that lives in the sea, swims, and has fins is a fish
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate 'where it lives' from 'what it is'. List mammal tests — breathes air, milk, warm-blooded — and apply them to the dolphin. It passes all three, so it's a mammal despite the fins.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — it lives in the sea and has fins, so it's a fish
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Calls the dolphin a fish; justifies by fins/swimming/living in water

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks whales and dolphins breathe underwater through gills like fish
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show a whale/dolphin surfacing and spouting through its blowhole — it MUST come up for air and would drown if held under. Contrast with a fish's gills.
errorPatterns.distractor: It breathes underwater with gills, like a fish
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Second tier: says it breathes underwater; doesn't know it surfaces for air

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks a mammal must live on land, so a sea creature can't be a mammal
errorPatterns.nextMove: Give the rule: a mammal is defined by breathing air, warm blood and milk — NOT by where it lives. Whales are sea mammals; bats are flying mammals. Home doesn't decide the group.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Accepts the milk/air facts but still refuses 'mammal' because it lives in water

responseLevels.gap: Calls the dolphin a fish because it lives in water / has fins; no mammal reasoning.
responseLevels.full: States dolphin/whale is a mammal and justifies with air-breathing (surfaces, no gills), milk-feeding and warm blood, AND explains that habitat doesn't determine the group — distinguishing it correctly from a shark (a true fish).
responseLevels.partial: Says 'mammal' but can give only one weak reason, or knows it breathes air yet still hesitates because it lives in the sea — the label without the full 'how you can tell'.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A dolphin lives in the sea, swims fast, and has fins and a smooth tail. A child says: 'So a dolphin must be a fish.' Is that right? Tell me what a dolphin really is, and how you can tell.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who has the concept says 'mammal' and gives an air-breathing / milk reason. A child holding the very common 'lives in water + fins = fish' rule says fish and justifies it by the swimming/fins. The second tier ('how can you tell?') is decisive: the mammal answer rests on breathing air and feeding milk, which a child reasoning only from habitat cannot supply.
